Chapters- The Johannesburg Library

By: Mart-Marie Faure | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
After half a decade the Johannesburg Library has opened its doors once more bringing hope to a crumbling inner city.

Unique Selling Point:
A new chapter has opened for the Johannesburg City Library after being closed to the public for half almost decade.
For five long years, 1.5 million books, including rare and valuable Africana archives, sat locked away, gathering dust. This year, the library turns 90 years old, a true continental landmark and one of the largest public libraries in Africa.
This reopening belongs to the caring citizens of Joburg, heritage groups, civil society, and activists who refused to accept closed doors fighting shoulder to shoulder with Johannesburg Heritage Foundation, Joburg Crisis Alliance, Johannesburg In Your Pocket City Guide, Bridge Books, and many others.
In an age of disinformation, inequality in digital access, and shrinking public spaces, libraries are more relevant than ever. They are lifelines for learning, safe spaces for community, and guardians of our shared heritage.
Hopefully this is the beginning of the re-awakening of a crumbling inner city.


Summary:
The Johannesburg Public Library (JCL), located in the citycentre, has a rich history dating back to the early days of Johannesburg. It began as a subscription library in 1890, evolving through various locations and ultimately becoming a vital public institution. A key moment in its history was the opening of its current Italianate building in 1935, and its later desegregation in 1974, making it the first public library in South Africa to open its doors to all races.

Script:


(Flo Bird) Books have their own feel and their own smell. And that's something, a special pleasure.

(Masa) For people like Flo Bird, who has been coming here since she was 3, the reopening of the Johannesburg City Library after lengthy renovations – and just in time for its 90th birthday – is reason for celebration.

(Flo Bird) It's looking beautiful, and they'd had everything dusted and cleaned and polished to do. It looked superb.

(Masa) It had been closed for five long years. And now, the iconic Johannesburg City Library has finally reopened its doors.

(Masa) With upgrades to the historic building complete and fire safety fully compliant, Senior Library Assistant Elton May takes us on a journey through its restored halls and rich history.

(Elton May) This is the renowned Africana collection – or the African Studies Library, as the name implies. The African Studies Library collects information about Africa, Southern Africa – specifically south of the Zambezi. People, places, history, culture. Anything to do with Africa and Southern Africa. For example, here we have the DRUM magazine which, as you know, is DRUM magazine.

(Masa) DRUM magazine?

(Elton May) A DRUM magazine. January 1964 to April 1965. So, all of those magazines for all that period of time is bound in one volume, because one of our mandates is the preservation of old printed material and to keep it available and usable for as long as we possibly can.

(Masa) There's something sacred about a book.

(Masa) I wish you could smell it. Sho.

(Masa) Not just in its pages, but what it represents – history, knowledge, lessons.

(Masa) Jeeze, Elton. I've never seen so many art books in my life.

(Elton May) Yes! Johannesburg City Library actually has two art libraries; a Performing Arts Library and a Visual Arts Library. This is the Visual Arts Library and it consists of a range of art styles, whether it's printing, painting, comic books, calligraphy…

(Masa) Wood sculpture.

(Elton May) Yeah, exactly. And they are allowed to sit here, use the material. They can even take the material out.

(Masa) Fashion.

(Elton May) Yeah, exactly.

(Masa) Wow.

(Elton May) So, this is the Performing Arts Library where we have material on movies, music sheet scores and so on and so forth.

(Masa) May I?

(Elton May) Yes, you may.

(Masa) Oh, it's been a while though.

(Elton May) Joburg City Library is actually an archiving library, which means that we don't throw anything away. As you can see...

(Masa) Clearly.

(Elton May) CDs and DVDs. We have got VHS tapes, Betamax, 8-track, vinyl.

(Masa) Wow.

(Elton May) So, this is the Reference Collection. It caters specifically for tertiary level students and researchers. And the books we have up here is for every subject from the occult rights down to history. The 26 000 books we have up here are actually the top of the iceberg. There are more than half a million books available downstairs in the archives, as well.

(Masa) A researcher's dream.

(Elton May) That's correct.

(Masa) Hidden four storeys underground, and spanning an entire city block, this extraordinary archive holds more than 3 000 unique journals and 600 000 books.

(Elton May) So, this is the oldest item down in the archives that we have. It's a family Bible. When this was brand new, it would have been leather, soft leather with what looks like brass hinges. But it's over 300 years old. You can have a look here – printed in 1730.

(Masa) Wow.

(Elton May) It's a very old item. Very, very valuable. The vast majority of the material available in Joburg City Library is physical paper-based. And for the library to stay relevant and to future-proof, as it were, we need to digitise our older, especially rare or one-off material that is only available here. But we have already made a start on digitising some of the information.

(Masa) For a bookworm like me, this is really exciting. It's more than just the doors of the library opening. It's the doors to opportunities opening, growth, learning and, for many of us, an escape.

(Masa) As many smaller public libraries remain closed, this reopening offers a glimmer of hope.

(Masa) You know, often, Flo, we talk about the ity's degradation. What do you think the upgrade of the City Library does for the renewal of the inner city of Johannesburg?

(Flo Bird) Well, I think it's very important because, you know, there's a book about the library called the Heart of the City, and I feel very much it is the heart. And the library has always been free, you know. The only charges you pay for are things like photocopies and a fine if you're late.

(Masa) Don't be late.
